abstract: Dr. Morgan reviews the epidemiology, safety, and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines for children aged 6 months to 5 years. Children in this age group have the highest hospitalization, ICU admission, and death rates among all pediatric age groups, with 46–68% of hospitalized children having underlying health conditions. The vaccine studies were small but well-designed, showing no myocarditis and rare febrile seizures, with local reactions worsening after the second dose. Efficacy ranged from 31–46% for Moderna and similar for Pfizer, and the vaccine is safer than COVID-19 infection in this population.
key_points: Children 6 months to 4 years have the highest hospitalization and death rates among pediatric age groups.
46–68% of hospitalized children in this age group had underlying health conditions.
COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths in this age group were as high or higher than for other vaccine-preventable diseases at the time their vaccines were developed.
The vaccine studies were observer-blind, placebo-controlled, and randomized, but small in sample size.
No cases of myocarditis were observed in the pediatric vaccine trials.
Local reactions (pain, redness, swelling) are common and may worsen with the second dose; Moderna reactions are generally worse than Pfizer.
Febrile seizures are a rare side effect (one case in the studies) but also occur with COVID infection.
Vaccine efficacy: Moderna 46% for ages 2–5 years and 31% for ages 6–23 months; Pfizer has similar percentages.
Pediatric COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer) for ages 6 months–5 years was studied under EUA with 2-month seropositivity and 7-month safety follow-up.
Vaccine efficacy is about 80% in preventing infection, but data are limited to a few months.
Antibody duration in children is inferred from adult data (about 3 months).
The highest risk of hospitalization is in the youngest age group (6 months–5 years).
